issues.legal_issue: A tenant is not barred from pursuing an appeal merely because the tenant requested time to vacate, unless the request or undertaking gave the tenant an advantage that would make it inequitable to permit the appeal.
material_facts: The tenants requested time to vacate, and the High Court granted time on condition that they file an undertaking.
The tenants did not file the undertaking and filed their appeal within the period of limitation.
The landlord did not show that the tenants had obtained an otherwise unavailable advantage.
issues.conclusion: The request for time did not estop the tenants from appealing, and the preliminary objection to maintainability was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: A request for time or an undertaking does not, by itself, foreclose statutory or constitutional remedies. Estoppel may affect the court’s discretion where the tenant obtained an advantage in reliance on the undertaking, but no such circumstances existed here.

rule.if: tenant_appeal_from_eviction_order and time_to_vacate_requested and not undertaking_given and appeal_timely

predicates.tenant_appeal_from_eviction_order: The tenant appealed an order directing eviction.
predicates.time_to_vacate_requested: The tenant asked the court for time to vacate the premises.
predicates.undertaking_given: The tenant gave an undertaking to vacate the premises.
predicates.appeal_timely: The tenant filed the appeal within the applicable limitation period.

issues.definition: When a tenant appealing an eviction order requested time to vacate but gave no undertaking and appealed in time, the request does not bar the appeal by estoppel.

issues.legal_issue: A prior decision between the same parties construing trust documents binds them on the construction decided in that proceeding.
material_facts: In an earlier proceeding between the parties, the landlord argued that the trust was governed by the religious-endowments legislation and that a civil trust suit was not maintainable.
The earlier court construed the trust deeds and held that they created a religious endowment or religious charity within the meaning of that legislation.
That construction was the basis for dismissing the application for leave to bring the trust suit.
issues.conclusion: The earlier construction of the trust deeds was res judicata and bound the parties.
issues.legal_principle: A determination of an issue between the same parties is binding in a later proceeding when that determination was necessary to the earlier decision. The earlier decision construed the trust deeds as creating a religious endowment or religious charity under the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959.

predicates.later_proceeding_between_same_parties: The later proceeding involves parties who were also parties to the earlier proceeding.
predicates.earlier_court_decided_trust_character: The earlier court determined the character of the trust by construing its governing documents.
predicates.earlier_decision_depended_on_that_determ: The earlier court relied on its determination of the trust’s character as the basis for its decision.

issues.definition: When the same parties return to court and the earlier decision depended on a determination of the trust’s character, that determination binds them.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that premises belong to a public religious or charitable trust cannot be rejected as unfounded where trust documents and a binding prior decision provide prima facie support for exemption from rent-control provisions, although the exemption’s final applicability need not be decided in the eviction proceeding.
material_facts: The tenants relied on registered trust deeds that included the premises, and the inclusion was admitted.
A prior decision between the parties had construed the deeds as creating a religious endowment or religious charity.
A government notification exempted buildings owned by Hindu, Christian, and Muslim religious public trusts and public charitable trusts from the rent-control provisions.
The Rent Controller did not address whether the Act applied to the premises, and the appellate authority found prima facie that the premises were covered by the trust and outside the Act.
The Supreme Court did not finally decide whether the Act applied to the premises.
issues.conclusion: The tenants’ claim to the exemption had prima facie support and was not patently wrong or unfounded; the final applicability of the Act was left undecided.
issues.legal_principle: Section 29 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 authorized exemptions by notification, and the notification exempted buildings owned by specified religious public trusts and public charitable trusts. Sections 5 and 108 of the Tamil Nadu Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1959 restrict ordinary civil-court jurisdiction over matters governed by that Act; sections 6(16) and 6(17) define religious charity and religious endowment. The notification’s constitutional validity had been upheld in S. Kandaswamy Chettiar v. State of Tamil Nadu. The court treated the trust documents and binding prior construction as prima facie support, without finally resolving exemption.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding under a rent-control regime.
predicates.trust_documents_include_premises: Documents creating or governing a trust include the premises in dispute.
predicates.prior_binding_decision_characterizes_tru: A binding earlier decision between the parties characterized the trust as religious or charitable.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding, inclusion of the premises in trust documents and a binding decision characterizing the trust as religious or charitable give prima facie support to a claim that the premises are exempt.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant may bona fide dispute a transferee landlord’s derivative title without being barred by the tenant’s estoppel to deny the title of the person who originally created the tenancy, and the rent controller may decide only whether the dispute is bona fide, not finally determine title.
material_facts: The tenants were originally inducted by a trust, not by the person from whom the respondent claimed to derive title.
The tenants relied on trust deeds that included the premises and challenged how the alleged predecessor obtained the premises and whether that predecessor could transfer them.
The respondent claimed to have purchased the premises from the predecessor and relied on the predecessor’s notice directing payment of rent to the respondent.
The Rent Controller relied on rent payments, rent receipts, a decree, and the alleged sale, but declined to examine the predecessor’s entitlement to transfer the premises.
The landlord had pleaded that the predecessor was the absolute owner and that the landlord had purchased that ownership.
issues.conclusion: There was a bona fide dispute as to title, so the Rent Controller lacked jurisdiction to hear and finally adjudicate the eviction application on that basis; the landlord remained free to seek a final determination in a competent civil court.
issues.legal_principle: Section 10(2)(vii) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 permits eviction for denial of the landlord’s title only when the denial is not bona fide; the second proviso to section 10(1) sends a bona fide title dispute to the civil court. Section 116 of the Evidence Act estops a tenant from denying the title of the landlord who inducted the tenant, but does not estop the tenant from challenging a later end to that landlord’s title or a transferee’s derivative title. J.J. Lal Pvt. Ltd. v. M.R. Murali explains that the controller determines bona fides for the limited purpose of identifying an eviction ground, while title is for the civil court. The controller must assess whether the dispute has prima facie evidentiary support and may not finally determine title.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and tenant_inducted_by_original_landlord and eviction_claimed_by_later_transferee and tenant_supports_derivative_title_challenge_with_evidence

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding before a rent-control tribunal.
predicates.tenant_inducted_by_original_landlord: The tenant entered possession under a landlord other than the person later claiming the right to evict.
predicates.eviction_claimed_by_later_transferee: The person seeking eviction claims an interest transferred from a later predecessor in title.
predicates.tenant_supports_derivative_title_challen: The tenant challenges how the predecessor acquired title or whether the predecessor could transfer it and supports that challenge with evidence.

issues.definition: When a tenant inducted by an original landlord supports an evidentiary challenge to the derivative title of a later transferee seeking eviction, the rent-control tribunal cannot finally adjudicate title.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord who pleaded an eviction claim on the basis of ownership cannot avoid a tenant’s bona fide challenge to that ownership by later relying on a broader statutory definition of landlord.
material_facts: The respondent pleaded that the predecessor was the absolute owner and that the respondent had purchased the premises from him.
The tenants disputed the title of both the respondent and the predecessor.
The High Court treated the respondent as a landlord because the predecessor had directed the tenants to pay rent to the respondent.
The respondent’s pleaded claim was ownership by purchase, not a claim to evict in some other capacity as a person entitled to receive rent.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred by sustaining the eviction claim on a basis outside the respondent’s pleadings.
issues.legal_principle: The statutory definition of landlord enables a person who is not an owner, but it does not permit a party who pleaded ownership to abandon that case and establish a different basis for relief. Under M/s Trojan & Co. v. R.M.N.N. Nagappa Chettiar, a decision must be based on the parties’ pleaded cases, not grounds outside their pleadings.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought an eviction proceeding before a rent-control tribunal.
predicates.landlord_pleads_ownership_as_basis_for_e: The landlord pleaded that the right to evict arose from ownership of the premises.
predicates.court_relies_on_unpleaded_capacity_to_su: The court sustained the eviction claim on a different capacity or basis that the landlord had not pleaded.

issues.definition: If ownership is the pleaded basis for eviction, a court cannot sustain the claim by relying on a different, unpleaded capacity.
